items.content:
RT @Kostastsale: A recent PhantomStealer infection I observed produced some very useful behavioral artifacts that I'd like to share for threat hunting inspiration👇

This is for PhantomStealer, but the browser-access pattern is what you will see across many everyday Windows infostealers. The way it staged, exfiltrated, and deleted the collected data is more specific to this case.

Here are a few threat-hunting opportunities for inspiration.

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟭:

Look for  processes opening browser files like:

...\𝙼𝚒𝚌𝚛𝚘𝚜𝚘𝚏𝚝\𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎\𝚄𝚜𝚎𝚛 𝙳𝚊𝚝𝚊\𝙳𝚎𝚏𝚊𝚞𝚕𝚝\𝙻𝚘𝚐𝚒𝚗 𝙳𝚊𝚝𝚊
...\𝙼𝚒𝚌𝚛𝚘𝚜𝚘𝚏𝚝\𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎\𝚄𝚜𝚎𝚛 𝙳𝚊𝚝𝚊\𝙳𝚎𝚏𝚊𝚞𝚕𝚝\𝙽𝚎𝚝𝚠𝚘𝚛𝚔\𝙲𝚘𝚘𝚔𝚒𝚎𝚜

Edge accessing these files is normal. Some random process doing it is a different story.

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟮:

It staged Chromium (Chrome, Edge etc.) and Gecko cred collection files into very obvious filenames under a local\temp directory:

• *_𝚙𝚊𝚜𝚜𝚠𝚘𝚛𝚍𝚜_*.𝚝𝚡𝚝
• *_𝚌𝚘𝚘𝚔𝚒𝚎𝚜_*.𝚓𝚜𝚘𝚗
• *_𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚍𝚒𝚝_𝚌𝚊𝚛𝚍𝚜_*.𝚝𝚡𝚝

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟯:

The files were created,  exfiltrated, and deleted within ~10 seconds.

You should be able to hunt for:

credential files created → outbound traffic → files deleted

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟰:

It allocated 3,050 bytes of unbacked RWX memory inside Chrome using 𝚅𝚒𝚛𝚝𝚞𝚊𝚕𝙰𝚕𝚕𝚘𝚌𝙴𝚡, followed by 𝚆𝚛𝚒𝚝𝚎𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚌𝚎𝚜𝚜𝙼𝚎𝚖𝚘𝚛𝚢 into the same region. Strong evidence of process injection activity.

!!👆All infostealers do this👆!!

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟱:

Look for workstations sending data over FTP or FTPS, especially from processes that have no legitimate reason to do so.  (𝘐𝘵'𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘮𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘵 𝘢 𝘥𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘥 𝘰𝘧 𝘦𝘹𝘧𝘪𝘭𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯, 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘛𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘮, 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦.)

This case connected to:

𝚏𝚝𝚙.𝚊𝚖𝚋𝚒𝚔𝚊𝚎𝚡𝚙𝚘𝚛𝚝𝚜𝚒𝚗𝚍𝚒𝚊[.]𝚌𝚘𝚖
𝟷𝟿𝟶.𝟿𝟸.𝟷𝟽𝟺[.]𝟷𝟸𝟻
Contextual PTR: 𝚜𝟹𝟽𝟹𝟿[.]𝚋𝚘𝚖𝟷[.]𝚜𝚝𝚊𝚋𝚕𝚎𝚜𝚎𝚛𝚟𝚎𝚛[.]𝚗𝚎𝚝

The session used explicit FTPS through 𝙰𝚄𝚃𝙷 𝚃𝙻𝚂, so the initial FTP negotiation was visible before the traffic became encrypted.

𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝟲:

It queried 𝚒𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚑𝚊𝚣𝚒𝚙[.]𝚌𝚘𝚖 to discover the public IP. That service is legitimate, but I don't know many environments that are using it in a legitimate way. Maybe I'm wrong so always baseline! The process making the request and everything happening around it are what matter.

The malware also created 𝙻𝚘𝚐_𝚂𝚞𝚖𝚖𝚊𝚛𝚒𝚎𝚜.𝚝𝚡𝚝 (see screenshot) with host information, public IP, malware configuration, and enabled modules. Unlike the temp credential files, it was not immediately deleted and was sent to the C2.

Interestingly, several features were disabled, including screenshots, file grabbing, anti-analysis, and debug mode. Startup, keylogging, and CryptoClipper were enabled.

Thanks to @elasticseclabs for the excellent telemetry and YARA detections:

𝚆𝚒𝚗𝚍𝚘𝚠𝚜_𝚃𝚛𝚘𝚓𝚊𝚗_𝚇𝚎𝚗𝚘_𝟾𝟿𝚏𝟿𝚏𝟶𝟼𝟶
𝚆𝚒𝚗𝚍𝚘𝚠𝚜_𝙶𝚎𝚗𝚎𝚛𝚒𝚌_𝚃𝚑𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝_𝚏𝟻𝟽𝚎𝟻𝚎𝟸𝚊

The latter identified a WoW64 “Heaven’s Gate” transition stub.

items.content:
RT @LxlxIxlxlxL: KnownDLLs is a trust boundary.

Forshaw's Object Manager research makes the primitive obvious: when a trust boundary is built from securable objects, the boundary is only as strong as the DACLs protecting those objects.

\KnownDlls contains the shared image sections used by every process for things like ntdll.dll, kernel32.dll, etc. Windows hardens the directory ACL, but the interesting part isn't necessarily the filesystem.

Object Manager namespace semantics still matter.

Symlinks. Handles. Inheritance. Namespace resolution.

If the mitigation protects the file, but the security decision is ultimately made in the object namespace, don't waste your time asking who can write System32.

Ask who can influence the objects involved in resolution.

That boundary is where things get interesting.

Reference:

items.content:
RT @HackingDave: It’s midnight. 

I stayed up intentionally even though I’m waking up at 6. 

The reason is midnight marks the birth of an incredible human being that changed my life. 

His name was:

Kevin Mitnick.

I have his picture in my walk in closet in my house, I see his face everyday and I miss him.

Kevin was instrumental on who I am today. 

When I released the social engineering toolkit, he emailed me from mitnick@gmail.com. He said dude love the work you’re doing if you ever need anything / hit me up anytime.

I had an oh shit moment. Was this really Kevin? I remembered watching the news when I was in high school and his entire career. He was a hero to me early on. I reached out, and mind you this was 2006. 

He responded back immediately with his cell. I talked to Kevin for hours.

After that we forged a friendship. Everyday we grew stronger. Many knew Kevin based on the news and his contributions and books to the industry. I knew Kevin for who he was: something that was obsessed with hacking, being the best, and would burn through the hours he had on engagements just because he wanted to own everything. Someone that just wanted to do the best he possibly could and help others around him.

Kevin was my hero. They say never meet your heroes. This is false. Kevin was more than I could have imagined from one human being and someone that deeply cared for his friends. 

I’ll tell you a story about Kevin. He asked me if I wanted to go see Aerosmith. He said I got some decent tickets - offer is yours. A time to hang with Kevin and see Aerosmith ? Absolutely.

What he didn’t tell me was we had backstage band member access. I literally hung out with Aerosmith with just Kevin and I as if we were part of the band. Got to talk to all of them, as they tuned their guitars, got to party with them. I could literally walk on stage with the band as if I was a member.

I said Kevin - dude were you going to tell me any of this? He said, I just wanted to see your reaction and excitement. 

That was Kevin. We lost Kevin to pancreatic cancer and it was devastating to the community, his family, and me. I remember him telling me early on when he got diagnosed. I told him dude you are Kevin Mitnick, you can absolutely beat anything. I believed it. 

Even in his last days, he was asking me to ship the latest rainbow tables to him - as he was on his last breath. 

Kevin was elite. He was one of the best hackers I had ever met. He never let those skills fade. He learned from the people he trusted, wanted to understand every aspect of the technical details. Again, he was elite. 

The dude fought so hard. Stayed strong. A few weeks before his death he came to visit me at my house and I took him for a Delorean ride. He seemed super healthy and we were confident he had beat it. Unfortunately- nature took his toll and he passed. 

I will always remember the impact Kevin had on me professionally but also how he made me a better human being. One of my best friends. It was never Kevin the celebrity he was, it was Kevin my best friend and one of the best human beings I have ever met.

I miss you everyday my friend. You have taught me so much and I will continue to help others just as you helped me. 

@kminx 

Kimberly / thank you for always being a friend to me. I know how much you suffered during this time and how much you stood next to Kevin during his most challenging times. You are blessed with Morty his son, and I know this kid will be the most elite hacker that has ever set foot on this earth. I wish only happiness for you and for Morty. He always has a spot at TrustedSec however I have a feeling he will not need that and forge his own path. 

Kevin, I think and pray for you everyday. 

Thank you and for the legacy you instilled on this industry and the people that you helped. You are gone for now, but the legacy you left will span generations. 

Until we meet again in the future my friend. 

Happy Birthday Kevin.

RT @unpacker: Amazing research led by NIS in collaboration with South Korean security vendors has been released on Lazarus campaign. After reading the reports, I noticed that each focused on different parts of the intrusion, leaving several technical links scattered across the publications.

To make the campaign easier to understand, I consolidated the technical findings from NIS, @AhnLab_SecuInfo @S2W_official @ENKI_official_X and PlainBit into a single end-to-end infection chain and infographic.

The consolidated view highlights:
▶️Initial access via 0-day/1-day buffer overflow vulnerabilities in South Korean financial security software.
▶️A four-stage PNG steganography workflow for shellcode delivery and key exchange.
▶️An almost entirely fileless infection chain leveraging process injection, Windows Registry Security values, and NTFS Alternate Data Streams.
▶️SIGNBT/Struggle and Brandoor (COPPERHEDGE) payloads, including the malware's self-protection mechanism that removes itself from disk during execution.

items.content:
RT @RFGroenewoud: Elastic Defend 9.5.0 now carries the taint state on Linux kernel module loading events.

I loaded Singularity (the stealthiest open source rootkit I know). On load, it hides from lsmod, /proc/modules, and /sys/module, resets the kernel taint mask to 0, and filters "taint" and its own name out of dmesg, journalctl -k, and klogctl.

Even though the system looked clean, detecting the tainted flag on the loading event already exposed it. 

What is even more suspicious? The endpoint recorded this module loading out-of-tree and unsigned. The live host says the mask is 0, and taint is sticky by design, so that needs explaining and is a good hunting reference.

One caveat, because this is not a rule to switch on blind: OE is also what a DKMS build, an out-of-tree GPU driver, or a third-party filesystem module produces. Baseline the modules you load on purpose, then investigate what is left. Enforcing module signatures shrinks it further, since an unsigned module then fails to load.

Rule PR and references in the reply.

items.content:
RT @HakaiOffsec: Rust is rapidly becoming the language of choice for red team tooling, implants, and security-critical software. Yet the offensive security ecosystem has almost no obfuscation tooling for it. Nearly every production obfuscator targets C/C++ binaries or operates on final PE/ELF images; Rust's unique compile pipeline, name mangling, and LLVM IR patterns require a fundamentally different approach. 

This talk presents Lyra, an open-source, cargo-native LLVM IR obfuscator for Rust. Lyra intercepts each crate during a normal "cargo build" via RUSTC_WRAPPER, transforms the LLVM IR with a configurable pass pipeline - string encryption, basic-block shuffling, indirect-branch obfuscation - recompiles the result with llc + clang, and substitutes the object before the real MSVC linker runs. Zero changes to the Rust compiler, zero changes to the target project's source code, one flag on the command line. 

We walk through the architecture, the engineering challenges unique to Windows/MSVC (UTF-16 response files, allocator-shim object preservation, inkwell's undocumented panic guards), and live before-and-after demonstrations in IDA Pro, Ghidra, and Binary Ninja. We also show a YARA rule that confidently matches a plain demo build returning zero results on the obfuscated binary, and two consecutive unseeded builds producing different hex patterns, defeating a rule written on the first build. Lyra is released open-source at the time of the talk. All demos are reproducible from the release. Attendees leave with a working tool they can run against their own Rust projects the same day.
